overview: In Jainism, the concept of mobile (trasa) and immobile (sthavara) beings is fundamental to understanding the nature of life and the practice of ahimsa (non-violence). Mobile beings possess two or more senses and include humans, animals, and other living entities capable of movement. They are considered to have higher levels of consciousness and are more complex in their interactions with the environment. Immobile beings, on the other hand, have only one sense, which is the sense of touch. These include entities like earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied, air-bodied beings, and plant life. The distinction is crucial in Jain ethical considerations, where harm to mobile beings is viewed as more severe due to their higher sensory perception and capacity for suffering. This classification guides Jains in their everyday actions, emphasizing minimal harm to all life forms to achieve spiritual purity.

primary_sources.title: Tattvartha Sutra
primary_sources.author: Umaswati
primary_sources.translation: Living beings are either mobile or immobile.
primary_sources.notes: This text is a key philosophical scripture in Jainism, outlining the fundamentals of Jain doctrine including the classification of living beings.

misconceptions.myth: All plants are considered non-living in Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: In Jainism, plants are considered living beings with a single sense (touch) and are classified as immobile beings. They are respected as life forms, and harm to them is minimized.
